source.title: Time is Not Compute: Scaling Laws for Wall-Clock Constrained Training on Consumer GPUs

page_placements.theme: Hardware, storage and deployment costs change practical scaling optima

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It measures validation loss across model sizes and training-time budgets and fits a wall-clock scaling relationship. This is a different setup from the cited compute-scaling studies and also reports how the fitted exponent changes with fitting choices.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own validation-BPB results, size/time sweeps, and scaling fits. The cited Kaplan and Hoffmann results in related work are background, not rows. The multi-architecture comparison is not a fixed-parameter-count comparison, so it does not test V4.
record.test_reason: Its own results bear on V5's repeated-data regime and on V7's fit-dependence, in a new setting: single RTX 4090s, a wall-clock budget, and a 48M-token dataset repeated up to hundreds of epochs. It does not test V1 or V3. The data bottleneck is deliberate, so V1's precondition fails. Size is optimised against wall-clock time, not FLOPs, so it is not a compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. In addition, the authors claim α = 0.60 ± 0.07 robustly exceeds Chinchilla's 0.50 across all sensitivity analyses, and attribute this to sublinear throughput (τ ∝ N^-0.8) and data-repetition penalties. They report a U-curve at every budget (it disappears at about 12h) and severe diminishing returns after the first hour. Their 'robust across all analyses' claim is undercut by their own 5-point fit (α = 0.44).
record.recipe_differences: The study replaces compute-budget scaling with a wall-clock-constrained sweep on consumer GPUs, uses validation bits-per-byte on a small dataset, and fits optimal size against time rather than reproducing the original compute-scaling recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponent changes with included time points and handling of the tied 2h optimum. The paper also reports changes in the loss-versus-size pattern across time budgets: U-shaped at short budgets, monotonic at about 12h, and U-shaped again at 24h.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed wall-clock budget on one consumer GPU, the optimal model size grows about as t^0.60 (8-point fit). The authors attribute this to throughput scaling as N^-0.8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Time-constrained optimal model size scales as a power of wall-clock time with an exponent above Chinchilla's compute exponent, set by hardware throughput scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Best achievable BPB vs wall-clock time follows L*(t)=1.223 t^-0.061 (R²=0.971).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On fixed hardware with finite data, best achievable loss falls as a shallow power law in wall-clock training time.

record.code_released: The paper says code, logs, and configurations are released; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The study uses one GPU type, one small dataset of approximately 48M tokens, one main architecture family, and no multi-GPU training. Most budget/model configurations are single runs; the three-seed check is limited to four models at 30 minutes. The authors note that the exponent may continue to change with longer budgets and that the 12–24h fits are not fully multi-seed validated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports many additional model-by-time validation BPB cells; these were not all extracted because of the 60-row cap and to prioritize the reported optima, non-monotonic outcomes, and fitting-choice results. Other omitted results include detailed throughput configurations in Appendix Table 3, marginal BPB changes in Appendix Table 5, and the individual seed values in Table 2; these do not add distinct tests of the fitted scaling-dependence claim beyond the rows retained.

untested.parts: All of it. The design makes data (48M tokens) a binding bottleneck and varies size and tokens jointly under a time budget. No loss-vs-N, D or C power law is fitted with the other factors non-limiting.
All of it. There is no extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
All of it. Optimal size is fitted against wall-clock time, not FLOPs. No token-count allocation law is fitted. The comparison to Chinchilla's 0.50 is across different independent variables.
All of it. Aspect ratio is fixed at 64, and the architecture comparison is not at matched parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer. No power-law fit in the repeated-data regime, only per-model loss changes with more repeated tokens.
All of it. There are no downstream tasks.
Effects of parameter counting, schedule, dataset or hardware on exponents, and the compute-optimal split specifically. Only point selection and tie handling are varied.

missing.what: Other Table 1 cells showing loss vs training time at fixed size under repetition (e.g. D10, D12, D16 across 4h–12h; D8 1h at 0.979, worse than 30min). These are relevant to the V5 repeated-data verdict.

record.verdict_notes: Single author, preprint, single runs at most budget cells. Token counts in the text conflict with Table 3 throughput: D24 at 5min is stated as 13M (throughput gives about 6M); D24 at 4h as 13M (about 290M); D26 at 24h as <3 epochs (about 9); D10 at 30min as ~5 epochs (about 9). The 'Chinchilla' comparison mixes time and FLOPs as independent variables, so it is not a V3 test. A depth law D*(t)=4.97 t^0.231 is also reported but bears on no version. Reader's V1 label is dropped because the study's design violates V1's 'not the bottleneck' precondition.

versions.untested_parts: It does not fit held-out loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute in a regime where the other factors are not bottlenecks. It reports validation BPB over model sizes at fixed wall-clock budgets, with bottlenecks and overfitting central to the design.
No test of whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
The study optimizes model size for fixed wall-clock time, not for fixed compute; it does not test both parameter and token counts as powers of fixed compute.
The reported architecture comparison does not establish comparisons at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies repeated exposure to a small text dataset, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds across repeated-data regimes or other modalities or training regimes.

The study varies fitting-point choices and discusses its dataset and hardware limitations, but does not systematically test alternative parameter-counting conventions, datasets, GPU types, or training schedules.

rows.subject: D24
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation BPB for a large model and the best smaller model at a fixed time budget.
rows.note: The paper attributes the poor result to low throughput and insufficient data processed.
rows.check: At 5min the larger model is token-starved, which is a data bottleneck V1 excludes, so 'reversed' is wrong. Also, the 13M tokens stated for D24 at 5min is inconsistent with the 20K tok/s in Table 3 (about 6M tokens).

rows.subject: D8
rows.operation_detail: Measured BPB at successive training durations for the same model.
rows.note: The paper describes the higher BPB as overfitting.
rows.check: Same model trained on more repeated tokens (2h to 4h, roughly 100+ epochs): BPB rises 0.906 to 0.925. This bears on the repeated-data regime, not on V1. Single run, no uncertainty.

rows.subject: D8
rows.operation_detail: Measured BPB at successive training durations for the same model.
rows.note: The paper says D8 had cycled through the dataset more than 250 times by 12h and describes further degradation.
rows.check: 0.919 at 12h is worse than 0.906 at 2h, so the baseline should be the 2h value. The paper's phrase 'degrades further' is inaccurate: 0.919 is slightly better than the 4h value of 0.925.

source_check.correct: D8: 0.906 BPB at 2h versus 0.919 at 12h. Table 1 also reports 0.886 at 8h. The 12h value is better than 0.925 at 4h.
source_check.problem: A shorter-duration baseline is explicitly available; the paper's description of further degradation from 4h is numerically inconsistent.

relationships.condition: Heavy data repetition (about 100+ epochs of a 48M-token FineWeb-Edu set, models 50M–621M, single runs)
relationships.reason: More repeated tokens stop helping or raise BPB: D8 0.906→0.925 (r10, r11), D14–D20 +0.005 to +0.012 (r15–r18), saturation or marginal change (r14, r19). Only D24, at fewer epochs, still improves (r20). So any repeated-data scaling form holds only up to a limited epoch count.
relationships.display_finding: Additional repetition raised BPB from 0.906 to 0.925 in one run and by 0.005–0.012 in others, while other tested runs saturated or changed marginally.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Heavy data repetition (about 100+ epochs of a 48M-token FineWeb-Edu set, models 50M–621M, single runs)
source_check.reason: Within the named 50M–621M condition group, r10–r11 and r15–r18 show worsening loss, while r14 and r19 show saturation or marginal change. These are absent or reversed effects under the verdict rules. D24 in r20 is outside this group, and its improvement does not establish a power law. The text quantifies 250+ epochs for D8 at 12h but does not establish about 100+ epochs for every model in the group.

relationships.reason: The exponent ranges from 0.44 to 0.805 depending on which time points are included and how the 2h tie is handled (r22–r29). The authors state regime transitions mean it may not be a pure power law.
relationships.display_finding: The fitted wall-clock allocation exponent ranged from 0.44 to 0.805 depending on included time points and treatment of the two-hour tie, and the authors cautioned that regime transitions could prevent a pure power law.

relation.reason: Its own repetition results bear on V5, and its sensitivity analyses directly test V7's dependence on fitting choices.

tranche.reason: The study reports results in a new setting: wall-clock-constrained training on individual RTX 4090 GPUs with deliberately limited, repeated data.

source_check.notes: Durations correspond to independent training jobs with learning-rate schedules scaled to each budget, so repetition effects are not isolated continuation experiments. Section 5.3's 0.44 estimate contradicts the abstract's claim that every sensitivity analysis exceeds 0.50.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope

reader_labels.reason: The reported size curves include non-monotonic outcomes and overfitting, rather than a uniform decreasing loss curve; the paper also says the 12h curve is monotonic while the 24h curve has overfitting. Rows r9–r21 show these patterns. The study does not establish the power-law form in a regime where other factors are not bottlenecks.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Optimal-size fits over the tested RTX 4090 runs and alternative selections of time points
reader_labels.reason: The fitted exponent changes with included points and tie handling (0.44 to 0.805 across reported variants); the authors also state that regime transitions may keep the relationship from being a pure power law over all time scales. Rows r22–r29 support fit-dependence and possible curve bending.
